narrative:
The model estimated a 54% chance that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above an even chance, but it was enough for the admission decision to be unfavorable: your application was rejected because the predicted risk crossed the school’s cutoff.

The decisive factor was your third-year class-rank decile. At 1.00, you were far below the accepted-student average of about 5.79. This was the single strongest influence and pushed the prediction most sharply toward bar-exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the next most important factor. At 3.00, it was close to the accepted-student average of 3.23, and it worked in your favor, pushing toward passing. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and also leaned toward passing; your score of 30 compares with an average of 37.18 among accepted students. Even so, those favorable signals were not strong enough to offset the much larger concern raised by your third-year rank.

To strengthen a future application, focus first on evidence that your third-year performance does not reflect your likely bar-exam readiness. Consider additional advanced coursework, a structured bar-preparation plan, academic references who can address your trajectory, and admissions counseling. Retaking the LSAT could also help if you can improve your score, and applying to programs that review applicants holistically may give your GPA and other strengths more weight.
